title: Pulse Laser Deposited GaFeO3 Thin Film Grown on FTO: Correlated Ferroic Orders and Strong Magnetodielectric Coupling at Room Temperature
authors: Ishita Jana, Sourav Sarkar, Soham Saha, Kalyan Mandal
abstract: Room-temperature single-phase multiferroics exhibiting coupled ferroelectric and magnetic order are promising candidates for next-generation magnetoelectric memory and spintronic technologies. Here, we report the growth of approximately 100.6 nm thick polycrystalline orthorhombic GaFeO3 thin films on fluorine-doped tin oxide-coated glass (FTO) substrates by pulsed laser deposition. Core-level X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals a reduced Fe2+ concentration and suppressed oxygen-vacancy formation, contributing to reduced leakage current and improved ferroelectric characteristics. The films exhibit robust ferrimagnetism and ferroelectricity at room temperature, confirming the coexistence of ferroic orders within a single phase. Piezoresponse Force Microscopy further demonstrates reversible local polarization switching, accompanied by an asymmetric butterfly loop with coercive voltages of -0.31 V and +1.07 V. The films also exhibit a high relative dielectric constant of approximately 1700 with a relatively low dielectric loss tangent of approximately 2.83 at 1 MHz. Moreover, a significant magnetodielectric coefficient of approximately 2.3% is observed under a relatively small magnetic field of only 0.1 kOe, highlighting strong magnetoelectric coupling. These results establish GaFeO3 thin films as a promising platform for room-temperature multifunctional devices, mainly low-field magnetoelectric memory and spintronic architectures.
summary: This work reports the successful synthesis of $	ext{GaFeO}_3$ thin films using Pulsed Laser Deposition, establishing them as promising room-temperature multiferroics. Key characterization confirmed the coexistence of ferroelectric and ferrimagnetic orders, alongside a measurable strong magnetodielectric coupling. These findings position $	ext{GaFeO}_3$ as a viable platform for advanced spintronic and memory devices.
main_problem: The research aims to develop room-temperature single-phase multiferroics exhibiting coupled ferroelectric and magnetic order for next-generation spintronic and magnetoelectric memory devices.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrated that $	ext{GaFeO}_3$ thin films exhibit robust ferroelectricity, ferrimagnetism, and strong magnetodielectric coupling ($\sim 2.3\%$) at room temperature.
method: The films were grown using Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) and characterized using a suite of techniques including X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), Piezoresponse Force Microscopy (PFM), and dielectric/magnetic measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is polycrystalline orthorhombic $	ext{GaFeO}_3$ thin films grown on FTO substrates. The focus is on the interplay between ferroelectric, magnetic, and dielectric properties within this single-phase material.
key_observables: Reversible local polarization switching (PFM), high relative dielectric constant ($\sim 1700$), strong magnetodielectric coefficient ($\sim 2.3\%$), and specific chemical ratios ($	ext{Fe}^{3+}/	ext{Fe}^{2+} \approx 1.65$).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, low magnetic field ($0.1 	ext{ kOe}$), and controlled stoichiometry (low oxygen vacancies).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the controlled growth conditions (PLD) lead to a stable, single-phase multiferroic material suitable for device applications.
figures_summary: Figures show XRD confirming orthorhombic symmetry, FESEM/SEM confirming film thickness ($\sim 100.6 	ext{ nm}$), PFM images demonstrating polarization switching, and spectra used to analyze chemical states (XPS).
paper_structure: The paper follows a standard materials science structure: introduction of the problem (multiferroics), detailed characterization of the synthesized film ($	ext{PLD}$ growth, $	ext{XPS}$ for stoichiometry, $	ext{PFM}$ for ferroelectricity), and finally, demonstration of the key coupled property (magnetodielectric effect).
why_interesting: While the core physics is condensed matter solid-state physics, the strong coupling between electric and magnetic orders ($	ext{magnetoelectric}$ effect) is a key area of interest in quantum materials research, linking classical ferroics to quantum phenomena.
